title: Inference, Cost and Latency Engineering
premise: The two questions a field engineer is actually asked in the room are what this will cost at our volume and how fast it will feel. Very few candidates can answer either with a number, and the ones who can are visibly different in the meeting. This course exists to make you one of them.
advanced_standing_note: Advanced standing awarded 1 of 3 credits, for token economics: Career Side Quests already carries per-run token accounting and routes mechanical stages to the cheapest capable provider. That covers measuring cost after the fact. It does not cover modelling cost before building, which is the half that matters in a customer conversation and is not exemptable here. Serving, batching, caching and quantisation carried over nothing.
hardware_note: Modules 4 and 5 need a GPU. The droplet cannot serve models — it is 1 GB running five services, and the analytics unit is already memory-capped to stop a parse from taking the apps down. The realistic options are a few rented GPU hours, or llama.cpp locally, which is enough for the quantisation work and for measuring the throughput-latency curve at small scale. Where an assignment can only be done at small scale, say so and state what you would expect to change at production scale — that judgement is itself assessed.
laboratory: Your own products, and one of them is unusually well suited: 1 Percent More Fluent streams both text and audio, so it has a real time-to-first-token problem with a real user on the other end. Career Side Quests is the cost case — a multi-stage pipeline with per-run accounting already in place.
sitting_rule: Every item is completable in one sitting. Nothing exceeds 180 minutes, and anything over 90 declares its own checkpoints.

panel.blind_note: Judges see the submission and the rubric, never each other's scores, and never the learner's self-assessment.
panel.disagreement: Scores are reported per judge and never averaged into a single number when the spread is 2 or more on any criterion.
panel.measurement_note: Latency claims must come with a distribution, not a single number. A submission reporting only a mean fails the blocking check before any judge reads it — the tail is the user experience.
panel.exemption_handling: An exempted item is recorded on the transcript as advanced standing at Tier 3 with its artifact link, never as completed coursework.

items.title: Transformer Inference Arithmetic
items.brief: Read this first and read it properly. It is first-principles arithmetic with no experiments and no hard maths, and it is the thing that lets you answer a costing question in the room rather than promising to follow up.

items.title: Inference (CS336 Lecture 10)
items.brief: The inference lecture from the playlist. Prefill and decode, the KV cache, batching and speculative decoding, all derived rather than asserted.

items.title: Instrument every call
items.exempt_rationale: Career Side Quests already carries per-run token accounting across every stage, and routes mechanical stages to the cheapest capable provider. Cite the implementation and its cost readout rather than rebuilding it.
items.brief: Make every model call in one product report its input tokens, output tokens and cost, aggregated per user-visible operation rather than per API call.

items.title: Cost model before you build
items.brief: This is the unexempted half. Pick a feature you have not built. Before writing any of it, produce a cost model: tokens per operation, operations per user per month, cost at 100, 10,000 and 1,000,000 users, and the single assumption the whole model is most sensitive to. Then build a thin version and compare the actual cost against your prediction. Report the error and where it came from.
checkpoints: model written and timestamped before implementation
predicted versus actual reported with the error explained

items.title: The fine-tune decision
items.brief: Should we fine-tune? is a top-three customer question and the honest answer is an arithmetic one. Take a real capability gap in one of your products and cost three routes to closing it: better prompting, retrieval, and fine-tuning. For each, state the engineering cost, the per-request cost at volume, the expected quality gain and how you would measure it, and what has to be true for it to be the right answer. You are not fine-tuning anything here — AIE-205 does that. You are learning to answer the question before the work, which is the part of it a field engineer actually owns.
items.optional_reason: AIE-107 M4.4 costs four routes over three years — frontier API, self-hosted open model, fine-tuned small model, and no model at all — and AIE-107 is studied first. This item costs three of those four and adds nothing AIE-107 does not already demand. Kept as an elective for the case where a specific capability gap is worth costing on its own; it is assessed if submitted, and completion does not wait for it.

items.title: Retention: token economics and cost modelling
Making Deep Learning Go Brrrr From First Principles
items.brief: Compute, memory bandwidth, overhead. The three-way split that explains why an optimisation helped, or did nothing at all.

items.title: Measure the split
items.brief: For one real feature, measure time to first token and inter-token latency separately across at least 100 requests, at three different input lengths. Show that prefill scales with input and decode does not, or explain why your data says otherwise. Report distributions — p50, p95, p99 — never a mean alone.

items.title: The latency budget
items.brief: Write the end-to-end budget for one user-visible operation: every hop, its measured contribution, and which hop you would attack first. Include the parts that are not the model — network, cold start, your own code — because they are frequently the majority and are always the first thing a customer's engineer will ask about.

items.title: Retention: prefill, decode and latency structure
litellm: routing, fallbacks and caching
items.locator: litellm/router.py — the routing, fallback and caching paths.

items.title: Cache what actually repeats
items.brief: Find the repeated prefix in one of your products — a system prompt, a rubric, a document read on every request — and cache it. Report hit rate, cost saved and latency saved separately, over real traffic rather than a synthetic loop. Then state the traffic pattern at which the cache stops paying for itself.
checkpoints: repeated prefix identified from real traffic
cost and latency savings reported separately

items.title: When the cache is wrong
items.brief: Describe the case where your cache serves something it should not have, how a user would notice, and what invalidates it. Every cache has one. A submission claiming otherwise must argue it.

items.title: Sarathi-Serve: taming the throughput-latency tradeoff
items.brief: Chunked prefill. This paper names the trade directly, and the trade is what a customer is really asking about when they ask how fast it is.

items.title: vLLM: scheduler and engine
items.locator: The engine and scheduler under vllm/ — start at the LLMEngine entry point and follow a request through.

items.title: Throughput versus latency, measured
items.brief: Serve an open model yourself — rented GPU or llama.cpp locally — and produce the curve: requests per second against p95 latency, as concurrency rises. Find the knee. If you can only run this at small scale, say so explicitly and state what you expect to change at production scale and why.
checkpoints: model served locally or on rented hardware
curve plotted with the knee identified

items.title: The curve a customer asks for
items.brief: Convert that curve into the answer to 'we have 500 concurrent users, what do we need?' — hardware, expected p95, monthly cost, and the assumption most likely to make you wrong.

items.title: Retention: batching, scheduling and the serving stack
llama.cpp: quantisation formats in practice
items.locator: tools/quantize/ and the quantisation format table in the README.

items.title: Quantise, and find what it cost you
items.brief: Take one model at two or more quantisation levels and measure three things on the same task: memory, speed, and quality against an eval set from AIE-102. The quality number is the one people skip and it is the only one that decides whether you can ship it. Report where the quality falls off a cliff rather than where it declines gently.
checkpoints: two or more quantisation levels run
quality measured against a real eval set

items.title: Retention: quantisation methods and their costs
Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
Time to first token, on the text path
items.brief: 1 Percent More Fluent streams text to a person who is waiting. Measure time to first token as the user experiences it — from their action, not from your API call — then make one change and measure again. Report the distribution before and after, and the cost of the change. Scope this to the text path only: the audio path is measured in AIE-106 M4.6, and measuring them together hides which one you actually improved.

items.title: Perceived versus measured
items.brief: Identify one change that made the product feel faster without making it faster, and one that made it faster without feeling faster. Explain the mechanism in each case. This distinction is most of what a good demo is made of, and being able to name it is what separates an engineer from a salesperson in the room.

items.title: Retention: streaming, speculation and perceived speed
Stability patterns
items.locator: The stability patterns and antipatterns - timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, fail fast.

items.title: Fallbacks, retries and routing
items.locator: The fallback and retry configuration, and the router's health-check behaviour.

items.title: Fail well
items.brief: Take a model-backed feature and make it degrade instead of breaking: a timeout that fires before the user gives up, a fallback to a different provider, a circuit breaker that stops hammering a failing endpoint, and a final deterministic answer that is still worth something. Prove it by breaking the primary provider deliberately and showing what the user sees at each stage. You have done this for payments; the difference here is that the fallback can be worse rather than merely slower, and the report has to say how much worse.
checkpoints: quality of the degraded path measured, not assumed

items.title: Retention: stability patterns for model-backed services
Ship a measured improvement
items.brief: Make one of your live products materially cheaper or faster, with the improvement measured on real traffic before and after. Materially means you would mention the number to a customer without embarrassment.

items.title: The economics report
items.brief: Write the document you would hand a customer evaluating this feature: what it costs per operation, what it costs at their volume, the p50 and p95 latency, what you tried that did not help, and the volume at which the architecture would have to change. Add the commercial frame a buyer actually uses: cost per interaction set against the value of that interaction, and the gross margin the feature leaves at their volume. A cost with no value beside it cannot be acted on.
checkpoints: cost per operation and at volume
cost per interaction set against value and margin

items.title: Publish
items.brief: Publish this as the next chapter of your public engineering log — one growing site, not a sixth standalone post. The chapter must stand alone on its own page for a reader arriving cold, and must connect backwards to at least one result from an earlier chapter. Publish at a stable public URL with the measurement harness reachable, so a reader can rerun the benchmark against their own setup.

items.title: Oral defense
items.brief: Three unscripted questions generated from your report at defense time, answered aloud without notes.
sample_question_shapes: A prospect has 50,000 daily active users. From your numbers, what do they spend a month and what do they feel?
Your p95 is three times your p50. Explain that to a customer who has just noticed it.
Which of your measurements would you least want a performance engineer to audit?

rubrics.anti_gaming: A model that predicts the actual cost perfectly is more suspicious than one that misses by 40% and explains why. Judges are instructed to weight the diagnosis, not the accuracy.

preconditions.check: 100 or more requests at three or more input lengths
p50, p95 and p99 reported — a mean alone fails
TTFT and inter-token latency reported separately

Every hop from user action to visible result, each with a measured number.
Reasoned by expected gain against effort, not simply by size.

preconditions.check: hit rate measured on real traffic, not a synthetic loop
cost saving and latency saving reported separately

levels.3: Found in traffic, with the repetition rate quantified before caching.
Derived from the measured hit rate and the cache's own cost, with the traffic pattern that inverts it named.

criteria.criterion: A genuine staleness case is identified

levels.3: Specific, with how a user would notice and how long the window is.
Event-based, with what happens to in-flight requests at the moment of invalidation.

p95 latency reported at each level

quality measured against an eval set, not judged by inspection

distributions reported before and after

One change isolated, with its cost reported alongside its benefit.

Explained in terms of what the user is attending to at each moment.

change is deployed and publicly reachable

levels.3: Clear, with the significance argued rather than asserted.
Quality checked against an eval set, and cost checked, both reported.

rubrics.anti_gaming: Making a product faster by making it worse is not an improvement. The quality check is blocking in spirit: a submission with no quality measurement cannot score above 1 on criterion 2.

levels.3: Every attempt reported with its number, including the ones abandoned early.
A volume given, with what breaks first at that volume.

levels.3: Answers with the number, the confidence and the caveat, unprompted.
Explains the mechanism and what could be done about it, with the cost.
Names one and says what would make it trustworthy.

rubrics.integrity: Assessed from the recording and transcript. Long pauses are not penalised; reading from a prepared text is.

levels.3: Three, each costed with the same rigour including the one the author already preferred.

criteria.criterion: Quality gain is estimated, not asserted

levels.3: Estimated with the measurement that would confirm or refute it named.
A decision with the specific condition under which it flips.

rubrics.anti_gaming: Fine-tuning is fashionable and is usually the wrong answer at this scale. A submission recommending it must clear a higher bar on criterion 2 than one recommending prompting, and judges are told so.

quality of the degraded path measured against an eval set

levels.3: Falls back, tells the user something true, and records which path served the request.

criteria.criterion: The cost of the fallback is quantified

completion.required: All non-exempt assignments and the project submitted. Exempted items are satisfied by citing the existing artifact and are recorded as advanced standing, not as coursework.
completion.grade_rollup: Deterministic. Each item's tier sets its weight; panel scores enter as per-criterion values; nothing is rounded up. Computed in TypeScript, never by a model.
completion.mastery_note: Sets initial mastery on the six inference skills. FSRS then decays them, so the transcript reports what is currently held.
